newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan unveils blueprint for securities reforms.
newsitem.headline: Japan unveils blueprint for securities reforms.

text.p: Japan on Friday unveiled a blueprint for reforms in the securities industry by 2000 and at the same time proposed harsher penalties against wrongdoing in financial markets.

The Securities and Exchange Council, which is advising the finance minister on the government's "Big Bang" deregulation, recommended a two-phase liberalisation of stock brokerage commissions, to be completed by the end of 1999, and the opening up of the securities business to new participants.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto announced his Big Bang reform plan last November to make domestic markets "free, fair and global" and compete more effectively against New York and London.
The council also urged Japan to break down barriers among banks and brokers in the second half of the 1999/2000 business year.

Allowing banks and brokers to enter the other's business sector was one of the toughest issues to resolve as brokers feared that they would lose their business to financially strong banks which have kept closer business ties with corporate customers based on cross-shareholdings.
The reforms are expected to be implemented two years earlier than originally planned, with the bulk of the deregulation measures to be taken within the current 1997/98 business year.
A Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said that 19 out of the 24 deregulation items linked to the securities industry and markets will be implemented by the end of next March.

Most of the five others will be carried out in the following financial year, he said, with the exception of steps related to stock-broking commissions and allowing the securities subsidiaries of banks to enter the stockbroking business.
In the proposals, the panel stated that Japan must establish a framework to enable securities houses to create innovative financial products by abolishing various regulations.

Behind the proposals for sweeping change lies the need to lure back to Tokyo businesses that have fled to escape high costs and excessive regulation, as well as a desire to force Japan's financial sector to boost its global competitiveness.
However, the move will inject strong competition into the brokerage business and may push some weaker brokerages, already battered by a slumping stock market, to the wall.

"The number of Japanese brokers will likely fall to half the current level over the next five to 10 years," an official at a major securities house said. "Many small brokerages are likely to close down or be liquidated due to increased competition."

Some analysts say revenues from commission fees will fall by at least 30 percent within one or two years of deregulation, while others say they could fall by half within the initial year of liberalisation.
The advisory panel also urged Japanese regulators to shift their focus to supervisory checks and away from using regulations as preventive measures.

To create fair and transparent markets, the council has also proposed that harsher penalties be imposed for illegal stock transactions, such as insider trading and stock manipulation, in line with global standards. It also called for stronger penalties for false statements by institutions to regulators.

The council also called for inspection, market-monitoring and penalty systems to be strengthened at Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), in order to deal with complicated new financial products and services which may be offered.
To help the domestic market compete more effectively with New York and London, it is not enough to merely copy financial products already offered in overseas markets, the panel said.
The securities watchdog was drawn into the spotlight recently by a payoff scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd that has once again sullied the reputation of Japanese brokers.
A key member of a the advisory panel told reporters the recent scandal involving Nomura Securities helped push forward proposals for financial reform in Japan.
